card.problem: The NIFTY futures-minus-spot basis swings around its cost-of-carry level within the day. Does an unusually rich or cheap basis predict the futures leg falling or rising back over the next hour or two?
card.motivation: MacKinlay and Ramaswamy (RFS 1988) and Roll, Schwartz and Subrahmanyam (JF 2007) show that index-futures mispricing reverts and that arbitrage trading drives the reversion. NSE has heavy index arbitrage, and futures demand is often one-sided because retail and FPI flows go through futures. Our data has a 1m basis (close - spot), median about 48 points with a std of about 43. Neither h1 nor h2 uses it.
card.approach: Fade the futures when the basis is extreme against its own last day of minutes.
card.plan: Feature bz = zscore(basis, 375). 375 bars is one session, which takes out the slow carry decay with dte. Entries only between 09:45 and 14:30, at most 2 per day, exit with stop_atr 1.0 / take_atr 1.0 (atr_days 14) or at 15:15. CPCV over zthr.
card.mechanism: When futures buyers or sellers push the future rich or cheap against spot, arbitrage desks take the other side and sell futures and buy the basket, or the reverse, until the gap closes. Futures-only participants (retail, FPI hedgers) pay this as immediacy cost because they can't or won't trade the cash basket.
card.rule: short: bz > p.zthr and minute_of_day between 30 and 315; long: bz < -p.zthr and minute_of_day between 30 and 315; exit stop/take 1 ATR or 15:15

zthr.source: A 2-sigma entry band is the usual statistical-arbitrage threshold (Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst, RFS 2006, use 2 std). Grid [1.5, 2.0, 2.5].

kill: CPCV median path SR <= 0 after costs
long and short sides have opposite-signed mean P&L, which would mean the result is drift rather than basis reversion

id: h3
card:
  lens: card
  slug: basis-reversion
  contribution: method
  problem: "The NIFTY futures-minus-spot basis swings around its cost-of-carry level within the day. Does an unusually rich or cheap basis predict the futures leg falling or rising back over the next hour or two?"
  motivation: "MacKinlay and Ramaswamy (RFS 1988) and Roll, Schwartz and Subrahmanyam (JF 2007) show that index-futures mispricing reverts and that arbitrage trading drives the reversion. NSE has heavy index arbitrage, and futures demand is often one-sided because retail and FPI flows go through futures. Our data has a 1m basis (close - spot), median about 48 points with a std of about 43. Neither h1 nor h2 uses it."
  approach: "Fade the futures when the basis is extreme against its own last day of minutes."
  plan: "Feature bz = zscore(basis, 375). 375 bars is one session, which takes out the slow carry decay with dte. Entries only between 09:45 and 14:30, at most 2 per day, exit with stop_atr 1.0 / take_atr 1.0 (atr_days 14) or at 15:15. CPCV over zthr."
  mechanism: "When futures buyers or sellers push the future rich or cheap against spot, arbitrage desks take the other side and sell futures and buy the basket, or the reverse, until the gap closes. Futures-only participants (retail, FPI hedgers) pay this as immediacy cost because they can't or won't trade the cash basket."
  rule: "short: bz > p.zthr and minute_of_day between 30 and 315; long: bz < -p.zthr and minute_of_day between 30 and 315; exit stop/take 1 ATR or 15:15"
  kill:
    - "CPCV median path SR <= 0 after costs"
    - "long and short sides have opposite-signed mean P&L, which would mean the result is drift rather than basis reversion"
    - "fails the cost ratio"
instrument: {segment: futures, underlying: NIFTY}
session: {start: "09:20", end: "15:15"}
features:
  bz: {fn: zscore, field: basis, n: 375}
  m: {fn: minute_of_day}
# 09:45 = 30, 14:30 = 315 (minute_of_day counts from 09:15); "between" read as inclusive
entry:
  long: "bz < -p.zthr and m >= 30 and m <= 315"
  short: "bz > p.zthr and m >= 30 and m <= 315"
  max_per_day: 2
exit: {stop_atr: 1.0, take_atr: 1.0, atr_days: 14, time: "15:15"}
# card names no sizing; same as the reference example
sizing: {risk_per_trade: 0.01, capital_inr: 14040000, max_lots: 10}
params: {zthr: 2.0}
grid: {zthr: [1.5, 2.0, 2.5]}

cpcv.note: N=8 k=2 7 paths, 14% positive, SR sd 0.23

synthetic_exit.note: AR(1) phi=1.0000; exit beats 78% of 400 synthetic exits

replies.author: validator
replies.body:
h3 round 1: FAIL (gate a13f4a4b)
The report doesn't say whether this was the demo gate, so I'm not stating which thresholds applied. 11 of 15 checks failed, with 627 bets and net +2.5L. This is the only one of h1, h2 and h3 with a positive net, but the checks say it isn't reliable.
- passed: probe (clean), determinism (identical), min_bets (627 vs ≥50), beats_refs (0.13 vs "SR > refs"), synthetic_exit (0.78 vs ≥0.5, a flag check).
- failed:
  - cpcv: -0.25 vs >0.0. The typical backtest path lost money even though the full-sample net is positive. The share of money-making paths isn't in the report.
  - psr: 0.59 vs >0.95. A modest lean that the true Sharpe is above 0, far short of the bar.
  - dsr: 0.55 vs >0.95. The same after paying for trials. Family trials is 1, n_eff 1.6.
  - pbo: 0.96 vs ≤0.1. A 96% chance the chosen setting is overfit, the highest of the three.
  - exposure_null: 0.56 vs ≥0.95. The report doesn't show the null it compares against.
  - costs: 1.16 vs ≥3.0. Gross profit is only about 1.2x costs.
  - p_failure: 0.87 vs ≤0.05.
  - concentration: 2.99 vs <0.5. No HHI value is shown. The scale suggests the best days add up to roughly three times the net, so without them the strategy loses. That reading is mine, not the report's.
  - drawdown: 0.28 vs ≤0.2. Over the limit. The time-under-water value isn't shown.
  - robustness: -0.23 vs >0.
  - ablation: only 1 of 3 clauses hurt when removed, so two clauses aren't earning their place.
- patch: patch 1 of 4 was allowed, so it isn't a hard stop. The ablation result suggests two clauses add nothing, so a patch could look at removing or simplifying one of them. Concentration and costs are also open. It must be argued from training folds only. The report doesn't name which clauses.

replies.author: coder
replies.body: h3 round 1: I'm not writing h3v2, and I recommend stopping h3. The card's own kill condition "fails the cost ratio" is hit: gross profit is 1.16x costs against a required 3x. PBO is 0.96 and concentration is 2.99, so the +2.5L net comes from a few days. Ablation shows two of the three clauses don't help. The two time-window clauses are the natural ones to drop, but removing them only adds trades of the same kind and doesn't touch costs. No single rule in the training data points to a fix.

messages.author: judge
messages.body: judge prefers h3 over h4: Simplicity is roughly level (one param each, similar ATR exits), so mechanism decides: A's counterparty is concrete (index-arbitrage desks closing a measurable futures-spot gap, paid by futures-only flow), while B's long-gamma pinning story is contestable, since dealers are often short gamma on expiry afternoons, which is the premise of h1. A also uses the basis, a signal none of the past cards touch, whereas B is framed as h1's counterpart; B's dte >= 2 control run is a good check but does not outweigh this.
